assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) took frequency metrology to the 1e-18 level and opened the way to a redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants. For someone who thinks in linewidths and measurement precision, this is the clearest case of a new measurement technique that changes what can be observed. The idea is original, the experimental demonstration is unambiguous, and the impact is broad.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Jun Ye's group drove the record accuracy and stability and the many-body clock physics. A two-person prize is clean. The ion-clock and comb communities (already recognised in 2005 and 2012) are separate. Whether others such as Lemonde, Ovsiannikov or Takamoto deserve mention is not resolved by the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent labs worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, others); performance continues to improve and the clocks are used operationally in comparisons. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the community's preferred credit ordering includes theorists of the magic-wavelength idea beyond the two names is uncertain; my recollection of the history is not independently verified.
The redefinition of the SI second has not yet happened, so the full practical payoff is still pending.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument for gravimetry, gradiometry, rotation sensing and measurements of the fine-structure constant and G. It is a decisive measurement method and directly relevant to the practical sensing applications (mineral prospecting, early warning) I regard as important. Part of the field was already recognised through laser cooling (1997) and the Ramsey/Ramsey-Bordé line of work is foundational.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's atom-interferometer concept with Ramsey-type separated fields, Pritchard's first atom interferometers with gratings, and Kasevich's light-pulse gravimeter and gradiometer all matter; the three-name configuration is plausible. Chu, Chapman, Mlynek and others also have strong claims, and the supplied credit does not include them, so the allocation is disputed.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many groups, with commercial and field-deployed gravimeters; large-baseline and space experiments are still developing, so the headline fundamental-physics reach is not yet realised.
uncertainties: Credit for the first demonstrations (Mlynek, Pritchard, Chu, Kasevich) is spread over more than three people.
Overlap with the 1997 prize and with Ramsey's method may weigh against it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale magnetometer and thermometer, with applications from nanoscale NMR to biology and condensed matter. The mixture of fundamental demonstration and instrument-level impact fits my emphasis on measurement.
assessment.attribution: Gruber/Wrachtrup (1997) showed optical detection of single NV spins, Jelezko and Wrachtrup showed coherent control, and Lukin's group developed much of the quantum-sensing and register concept work. The three given names form a reasonable trio, though Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth and others are also strong claimants and the cut is contested.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by a large number of groups; commercial sensors exist. Sensitivity claims and real-world advantage over classical sensors in specific applications are still being established.
uncertainties: Several equally important contributors are omitted from the supplied credit.
Practical advantage over established magnetometry in many applications remains to be shown.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid-Mott transition, Fermi-Hubbard physics and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This is a clean, controllable platform that has opened a field and lets one measure what condensed-matter experiments cannot. It follows the BEC prize in logic but is a distinct advance.
assessment.attribution: Greiner-Mandel-Hansch-Bloch (2002) is the central experiment; Bloch, Esslinger and Greiner led the experimental programmes; Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation and are theorists with a strong claim as well. With four credited, a three-name choice leaves out either Zoller or an experimentalist, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups; quantum gas microscopes are widespread. The scientific payoff for solving open problems such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram at low temperature is still partly pending.
uncertainties: Dropping Zoller (whose theory proposal is foundational) is a judgement call.
Whether the simulation results have yet answered an open condensed-matter question is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: EIT and the associated slow and stopped light are conceptually elegant coherent control of light with a quantum interference effect, and have become a standard tool for quantum memories, narrowband filters and nonlinear optics at the single-photon level. I know the field well from rare-earth slow-light work and see its influence on later quantum-memory approaches.
assessment.attribution: Harris developed EIT theory and the first experiments (Boller, Imamoglu, Harris 1991), and Hau demonstrated the 17 m/s slow light and later light stopping. Imamoglu's claim on the original EIT work is real, and Fleischhauer, Lukin, Phillips and Walsworth also contributed to stopped light, so the credit has an unresolved allocation.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed in many media (atomic vapours, cold atoms, crystals); the physics is stable. Applications are still mostly laboratory-scale, so impact outside physics is limited.
uncertainties: Allocation among Harris, Imamoglu, Hau, Fleischhauer, Lukin and Phillips is disputed.
Practical device impact beyond the lab is limited so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light is now routinely injected into gravitational-wave detectors to beat the shot-noise limit, an unusually concrete case of a quantum optical technique improving a measurement that matters. The theoretical idea is original and the demonstration is increasingly clear. It aligns with my view that measurement-limit advances matter.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 proposal for squeezed-state interferometry, Kimble's group made the first squeezed-state generation with Slusher and Wu (Slusher is not in the supplied credit), and Schnabel led the practical GEO600 and LIGO implementations. Walls, Yuen, Slusher, McKenzie and Lam also matter, so allocation is not settled.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in GEO600, LIGO and Virgo, with reproducible sensitivity gains. Timing is plausible now, though some may prefer to wait for a gravitational-wave-linked prize context.
uncertainties: Missing credited names such as Slusher and Walls complicate a fair three-person configuration.
Overlap with the gravitational-wave prize of 2017 may be argued either way.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade gave controllable strong interactions between neutral atoms, now the basis of programmable arrays of hundreds of atoms for quantum simulation and gate-based computation. The experimental demonstrations of blockade, entanglement and tweezer arrays are impressive and rapidly improving.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch/Lukin proposals and Saffman's gate work, together with Browaeys's and Gaetan's blockade demonstrations and Lukin's array experiments, make a plausible trio; Weiss, Bernien and others are also involved. The credit is spread and not fully clear.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups confirm the results, but the field is still moving fast, and fault-tolerant or application-level advantage is not yet established, so this looks a little premature.
uncertainties: Premature relative to a field still evolving quickly.
Credit is shared among theory proposals and several experimental groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter interfaces (quantum memories, repeaters, atom-photon entanglement) are a conceptual foundation of quantum networks, with the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller protocol and Kimble's networking vision as central ideas. I know the experimental difficulty from quantum memory work and note that efficient, long-lived, multimode memories remain a work in progress.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made foundational proposals, and Kimble demonstrated key experiments in cavity QED and quantum-network elements. Many experimental groups (Polzik, Lvovsky, Gisin, and my own field's rare-earth groups) contributed, and the prize configuration could be argued either way. I should also declare my own subfield proximity.
assessment.maturity: Individual elements are confirmed, but a functioning quantum network or repeater has not yet been demonstrated at scale, which makes recognition somewhat premature. A broader field-level prize would need clearer boundaries.
uncertainties: Full quantum repeaters remain a goal; the discovery is compound and its parts may deserve different recognition.
Potential conflict of perspective due to my own work on quantum memories.
